meta.description: Scarlett O'Hara says "never BE hungry again" — not "go hungry." And the vow isn't the film's: Margaret Mitchell wrote it in Chapter XXV of her 1936 novel.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'As God is my witness, I'll never go hungry again!'?
meta.ogDescription: The 1939 film says "never BE hungry again." And it borrowed the vow from Margaret Mitchell's 1936 novel — verified against the original text.

answer.label: Not quite — the actual line is “I’ll never be hungry again”
answer.authorDates: 1900–1949 · Atlanta journalist & novelist · Pulitzer Prize for Fiction, 1937
answer.sourceLine: Scarlett O’Hara’s vow in Gone with the Wind (1939) ends “As God is my witness, I’ll never be hungry again!” — not “go hungry.” And the film did not invent it: the vow is Margaret Mitchell’s, written into Chapter XXV of her 1936 novel, where Scarlett says “I’m never going to be hungry again.” The screenplay, credited to Sidney Howard, tightened her sentence; the public then loosened it back into a phrase nobody wrote.

source.excerpt: As God is my witness, as God is my witness they’re not goin’ to lick me. I’m goin’ to live through this and when it’s all over, I’ll never be hungry again. No, nor any of my folk. If I have to lie, steal, cheat or kill. As God is my witness, I’ll never be hungry again!
trail: 1936 — Margaret Mitchell publishes Gone with the Wind (Macmillan, 30 June). Chapter XXV ends with Scarlett’s vow: “as God is my witness, I’m never going to be hungry again.” Confirmed against the complete text ↗. The novel wins the 1937 Pulitzer Prize for Fiction ↗.

1939 — The film adaptation premieres in Atlanta on 15 December, compressing Mitchell’s sentence to “As God is my witness, I’ll never be hungry again!” Wikiquote’s transcription ↗ records the full speech. Sidney Howard ↗, who died that August, takes sole screenplay credit and becomes the first posthumous Oscar winner.

2005 — The American Film Institute places the line at #59 on its 100 Movie Quotes list ↗, printing it as “As God is my witness, I’ll never be hungry again” — a second independent record of the wording.

Since — The idiomatic “never go hungry again” spreads through repetition. It matches no line in either the novel or the film; the substitution appears to be ordinary memory smoothing an unidiomatic phrase, not a documented mishearing.
source.excerptNote: That is the 1939 film, verbatim. Mitchell’s 1936 original, which closes Chapter XXV, runs: “Hunger gnawed at her empty stomach again and she said aloud: ‘As God is my witness, as God is my witness, the Yankees aren’t going to lick me. I’m going to live through this, and when it’s over, I’m never going to be hungry again. No, nor any of my folks. If I have to steal or kill—as God is my witness, I’m never going to be hungry again.’” Both say be hungry. Neither says go hungry.

source.rightsNote: Both works are firmly in copyright in the United States. The novel was published in 1936 and its copyright renewed in 1964; because works published in 1931 or later can remain protected for up to 95 years from publication, it remains under US copyright ↗ and is not public domain in the US — it is public domain in Australia and other life-plus-50 countries only, which is why a complete text is lawfully hosted at Project Gutenberg Australia. The 1939 film is likewise in copyright; screen writing is work-for-hire, so the rights sit with the studio — Turner Entertainment ↗, which acquired the MGM library in 1986 — and not with Sidney Howard’s heirs.

author.name: Margaret Mitchell
author.heading: Who actually wrote the vow
author.metaLine: 1900–1949 · Atlanta journalist & novelist · Pulitzer Prize for Fiction, 1937
author.bio: Margaret Mitchell was an Atlanta-born journalist who wrote for the Atlanta Journal’s Sunday Magazine from 1922 until an ankle injury ended her newspaper career. She spent roughly a decade writing her only published novel, Gone with the Wind (Macmillan, 30 June 1936), which won the 1937 Pulitzer Prize for Fiction and has sold more than 30 million copies. Scarlett’s hunger vow — the line the 1939 film made famous — was hers first, on the page, three years before Vivien Leigh spoke a compressed version of it.

copyAttribution: "As God is my witness, I'll never be hungry again!" — Scarlett O'Hara in Gone with the Wind (1939), screenplay credited to Sidney Howard, compressing Margaret Mitchell's vow from Chapter XXV of her 1936 novel. The popular "never go hungry again" is a misquote.

misattribution.heading: Two errors, not one
misattribution.intro: The popular version gets the words wrong and gives the credit to the wrong work. Both are worth separating, because only one of them is the public’s fault.

items.why: No such line exists. The film transcript ↗ reads “As God is my witness, I’ll never be hungry again!”, and the American Film Institute quotes it the same way in ranking it #59 of the top 100 movie quotes ↗. Mitchell’s novel likewise says “be hungry.” The word “go” appears in no version of the vow.

The vow is credited to the movie almost universally, but it is Margaret Mitchell’s. Chapter XXV of the 1936 novel ↗ reads: “As God is my witness, as God is my witness, the Yankees aren’t going to lick me… I’m never going to be hungry again.” The screenplay contracted her sentence; it did not originate the line.

Scarlett is a fictional character and Vivien Leigh is the actress who performed the line — neither wrote it. Quotation sites routinely file the vow under “Scarlett O’Hara quotes,” which credits a person who does not exist.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest line: Margaret Mitchell wrote the vow in her 1936 novel ↗; the 1939 screenplay, credited to Sidney Howard ↗, compressed it to “As God is my witness, I’ll never be hungry again!” — and the public added the “go.”

context.heading: Why the drift happened
lead: The scene is the end of the film’s first half: Scarlett, starving in the ruined fields at Tara, retches, rises against a blood-red sky and swears an oath. It is the hinge of the story — the moment the spoiled belle becomes the survivor who will do anything. Curtain, intermission, and the line goes out into the culture.

“Never go hungry” is the more idiomatic English phrase, and idiom is a strong current. Memory quietly swaps the odd, flat construction Mitchell actually wrote — be hungry, a state, a condition, something you are — for the smoother thing we’d say ourselves. But the swap costs the line its meaning. To “go hungry” is to miss meals. To be hungry is what Scarlett has become, and what she is vowing to stop being.
context.detailsSummary: The other half of the error: what the film actually contributed
detailsBody: Mitchell, Chapter XXV (1936): “As God is my witness, as God is my witness, the Yankees aren’t going to lick me. I’m going to live through this, and when it’s over, I’m never going to be hungry again. No, nor any of my folks. If I have to steal or kill—as God is my witness, I’m never going to be hungry again.”

The film (1939): “As God is my witness, as God is my witness they’re not goin’ to lick me. I’m goin’ to live through this and when it’s all over, I’ll never be hungry again. No, nor any of my folk. If I have to lie, steal, cheat or kill. As God is my witness, I’ll never be hungry again!”

The screen changes are real but small: “the Yankees” becomes “they,” “I’m never going to be” contracts to “I’ll never be,” “steal or kill” widens to “lie, steal, cheat or kill,” and “folks” loses its s. This is the same pattern as the film’s most famous line: Mitchell wrote “My dear, I don’t give a damn” and the screen added “Frankly.” The movie sharpened Mitchell; it did not write her.

Who did the sharpening cannot be pinned to one hand. Sidney Howard holds the sole screenplay credit and won a posthumous Academy Award for it, but producer David O. Selznick rewrote substantially and Ben Hecht, Jo Swerling, Oliver H. P. Garrett, Barbara Keon and John Van Druten all worked the script uncredited.
context.pull: Mitchell wrote a state of being. The public keeps rewriting it as a missed meal.
